"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
Tales of Kieran<BR>
Vegepythicus, editor<BR><BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
[Librarian's Note ...<BR><BR>
The recorded tales of Kieran the Bard fall into three categories: the Woodland Cycle, Castles and Kings, and an unnamed cycle of lusty tales (recently destroyed by mysterious accident). Some are in the bard's own hand, while others, mere shadows of the originals, remain only as bedtime tales for children. The structure exemplifies the helical form favored by listeners about the hearth on a long winter's eve. As to whether they describe real events, be allegory, or be mere entertaining fancy, the reader must decide.]<BR><BR><BR>
I.<BR><BR>
Kieran was on the road from Wren to Fairtree, when he grew weary from the midday sun. His boots were tight and he thought to remove them for a bit in the shade of a nearby oak (oaks being a favorite of bards). This particular oak was venerable and gnarled, with sturdy branches that dipped and swooped, nearly touching the ground in spots. From its shade Kieran watched the forest creatures playing in the warm sun. But for the rustling of leaves, high above, the only sounds were of butterfly wings and birdsong.<BR><BR>
"What a peaceful day," Kieran thought as he watched a butterfly drift by, "What a beautiful day! In truth, since bards first told tales, has there ever been a day more peaceful and beautiful than this?"<BR><BR>
He drank from his waterskin and, taking his lute from its sack, cleared his throat and began to sing:<BR><BR>
"Oh, the maidens of Wren are passing fair ...<BR><BR>
...with breasts like melons, and flaxen hair ..."<BR><BR>
He had just taken a deep breath to bellow the lusty chorus when a small, feminine voice said, "Kind sir ..."<BR><BR>
He leaped to his stockinged feet, his face flaming red. "Who's there?" he cried.<BR><BR>
The small voice repeated, "Please, sir, if you will be so kind ..."<BR><BR>
Kieran looked about but saw no person or creature addressing him.<BR><BR>
"Pray thee," he cried. "Show thyself or have cause to fear my dagger." (He tried desperately to remember where he had last seen it.) "Whether thee be friend or foe, pray thee show thyself now."<BR><BR>
The small voice replied from above him, "Kind sir, thou hast no cause to fear me, and I am in need of help. Can thou find it in thy heart to aid me?"<BR><BR>
He looked up and saw naught but a small robin's nest, three branches above him. Climbing swiftly, he found a robin with three tiny robinlings, their mouths open wide.<BR><BR>
"Good mother robin," he asked, "Can it be thee who addresses me thus?"<BR><BR>
"Kind sir," she replied, "I have hurt my wing and it will be at least a day before I might fly. If my children do not eat soon, they will die. Would you be so kind as to bring a fat, juicy meal? Would you find a caterpillar or earthworm or grub for my children?"<BR><BR>
Now, Kieran was kind of heart and it was not within him to refuse a plea such as this, so off he went into the forest. Searching under some mulberry leaves, he soon found a small green caterpillar. It seemed a perfect meal for young robins.<BR><BR>
Plucking it from the leaf upon which it fed, he prepared to hurry back to the oak when he heard a tiny voice. He opened his hand and the caterpillar looked up at him with her big brown eyes wide with fear. "Kind sir," she said, "wouldst thou kill me so thoughtlessly?"<BR><BR>
Kieran scratched his head in puzzlement and the caterpillar continued: "When thou cooled thy feet beneath the oak, didst thou not find joy in my parents' beauty as they danced before thee in the sun? I, too, am soon to change. Wouldst thou deny thy successors the joy of my dancing? And if I do not live to have children, how will thine own children find such joy? Please, sir, would not an earthworm serve the needs of the robinlings just as well?<BR><BR>
Kieran looked into the eyes of the caterpillar and knew that he could not feed her to the robins. Carefully, he placed her beneath her mulberry bush and continued his search.<BR><BR>
Near a rushing brook, Kieran found a flat stone that, when moved, revealed a juicy earthworm enjoying the cool moist earth. "Aha." he thought. "As nice as the caterpillar may have been, this truly seems a more fitting meal for young robins."<BR><BR>
He had no sooner plucked the earthworm from it's cool abode (where it had been frantically trying to burrow away from him), when he heard a voice so faint he might have imagined it:<BR><BR>
"Kind sir," he thought he heard, and Kieran looked in his hand. The worm continued: "I am but a lowly creature, it's true, but might I plead such case that I have?"<BR><BR>
Kieran rolled his eyes skyward as the worm sat up and seized its chance. "I am not a lowborn worm like others you might find. No, I am a prince among earthworms. I come from an ancient lineage. My ancestors burrowed the earth when fires belched from black pits throughout these lands. I command millions like myself. Were it not for my loyal followers, you, good sir, would be up to your neck in leaves, tree trunks and mouldy carcasses. I'll make a bargain with you. If you release me and choose, instead, a pathetic grub for the robinlings, I will dispatch an entire clan of earthworms to keep your foreyard clean and sweet-smelling for as long as ye shall live." The earthworm looked hopefully at Kieran (while calculating the distance to the ground). "Good sir, what say ye?"<BR><BR>
Kieran was beginning to lose his patience, but, seeing the value of the earthworm's offer, decided that a grub would, indeed, make a tasty morsel for the young robins. He returned the earthworm to its moist haven and carefully replaced the flat stone above it. And, true to his desire, a short while later, in a forest glade, beneath a wide slab of discarded bark, Kieran chanced upon that which he sought: a fat white grub that would grow the robinlings into beautiful songsters. He plucked it from its hiding place and set forth. It was a beautiful day, indeed.<BR><BR><BR>
II.<BR><BR>
Nearby, in stately Trowbridge, King Caladan did live with his lovely daughter, Einlea. The princess was the apple of the old man's eye and the crown jewel of his small kingdom. He looked upon her with the blind pride of a doting father, and she, for her part, did naught but bask and flourish in his bounty.<BR><BR>
Trowbridge was quiet now, the chief sounds being the clatter of cart wheels and the cries of street vendors, but it was not always so. Three years earlier there had been trouble with Carthan to the west. It was not much, a border dispute, but the king persuaded a wizard named Loziard to come to Trowbridge in his employ, to aid him in the contest. Loziard was unknown by all in Trowbridge and kept to himself within the palace, coming and going as he pleased. When Trowbridge prevailed, with almost no loss of life, there was joyous celebration for days and weeks thereafter. Time passed, yet Loziard remained. The King, not wanting to seem ungrateful, said nothing, but became increasingly discomforted with the wizard's presence and wished for his departure.<BR><BR>
On Einlea's twentieth birthday, King Caladan called for a celebration and holiday through all his land. Unknown to his subjects, he intended to proclaim his retirement and the transference of his crown to his beautiful daughter. Out of politeness, and nothing more, he invited the wizard Loziard to aid him in devising a proper speech.<BR><BR>
Loziard was furious. He paced his chamber, his black brows knitted with intensity that would have soured any cow's milk. "Why," he cried aloud, "am I treated so unjustly by the old buffoon? Were it not for my skills, the border contest, mayhaps even the kingdom itself, might have been lost. I deserve more. I deserve the crown. To give it to that primping simpering daughter of his, who thinks naught of more than her own whim, is a slap more stinging than that of gauntlet. I will have justice. I will demonstrate, amply, for all to see, wherein lies true power."<BR><BR>
Thereupon, Loziard made his preparations.<BR><BR>
Princess Einlea's birthday came on a summer morning. Everyone within the city, and from the farms without, gathered to the palace for the festival. Banners waved from every rooftop. Fiddlers fiddled and dancers danced. Bakers baked wonderful sweets for the occasion. It was a day long to be remembered.<BR><BR>
At noon, precisely, King Caladan and Princess Einlea emerged onto the main balcony to the cheers of the kingdom. "Good citizens of Trowbridge," called the King, "We are but a tiny kingdom, but we prosper, do we not?"<BR><BR>
Loud hails (mostly) erupted from the crowd below. Encouraged, Caladan continued, "But now I am an old man. The day has arrived when younger blood can better attend to the needs and events of the kingdom. My subjects ... My loyal subjects and friends ... It is with honor ...and pride ...and the greatest of expectations ...that I transfer my kingdom and my crown to my loving daughter. To one and all, I give you" (a long pause here) "Einlea."<BR><BR>
As cheers filled the air, Caladan made a grand, sweeping gesture with his arm, intending to make the presentation as spectacular as the pride that filled him. His robe went "swoooosh" and his hand pointed to ... nobody. What was this? Where had she gone? Where Einlea had been, moments earlier, there now was naught but vacant air.<BR><BR>
"Er ...Einlea ...?" he called, uncertainly. But there was no response. Silence fell over park and courtyard. People glanced at each other nervously.<BR><BR>
Old Loziard clapped his hands in glee. He danced. He hugged himself with uncontained laughter. "How wonderful ..." he cried. "What a breathtakingly stunning and talented a wizard I am.." For what he had done, of course, was to rid himself of Einlea for once and for all. With one stroke, crafty and evil, he had removed the vain creature from the palace. Nought else remained between him and that which he desired.<BR><BR>
Now, magic is a tricky thing. Like all forces in the world, it must be kept in balance. As surely as day balances night and summer balances winter, so too must positive magic balance negative. For every hurtful or destructive spell, there must be an act of equal goodness or charity lest trouble overflow into the world. For every black wizard, there must be a white. For every spell of combat destruction, there must be healing. Know ye this ...if all who practice magic cast naught but healing or protective spells, dark, horrible forces would build up until chaos and ruin would burst forth and rain our doom down upon us. Thus may spells of healing be broken by harm, and the worst of spells be broken by charity.<BR><BR>
Knowing this, Loziard planned well his act of vengeance. To permanently rid himself of Einlea (short of killing her outright) he must devise a spell so cunning that no act of kindness would ever break it. He was pulling lice out of his long beard, late one evening, when he burst into laughter. He would make her into something ...disgusting.<BR><BR>
"I will make her into a frog." he laughed, then frowned. No ... that had been done. People might expect it and go around, like mindless idiots, seeking frogs, hoping to earn a kings ransom.<BR><BR>
And then, a brilliant plan occurred to him.<BR><BR>
"I will make her into a bug, an insect, a WORM ..." He almost choked on his wine. "Oh. How perfect.. I will make her into something so truly loathsome that she will spend the rest of her little bug life in terror of being squashed by the first person who sees her." He squealed and his rings jangled and his fat jiggled and he snorted wine out his nose in laughter. "Oh, how absolutely delicious ..."<BR><BR>
And that's exactly what he did. While King Caladan and his subjects scratched their heads in puzzlement, nobody saw a small fat white tree grub plop to the cobblestones beneath the main balcony and immediately curl up, glistening and quivering.<BR><BR><BR>
III.<BR><BR>
Einlea was terrified. What had happened? Well, she had seen enough of Loziard's magic to know what had happened. But why? Why would he do this to her? She didn't have long to ponder the question. A huge black hound, hundreds of times her size, ran to the cobblestone where she lay, and almost gobbled her with one slurp of his tongue. From somewhere, she found the wherewithal to roll out of his way and into the crevice between the stones. His HUGE slurpy tongue followed her, drooling and panting great hurricanes of hot awful breath down at her. But just as the tongue was about to lick her into the waiting stomach, the hound's owner yanked his massive chain and pulled the beast toward home.<BR><BR>
It is true that Einlea, in her life as a human, was self indulgent and not inclined to effort or resource, but that was merely because she had no need of either. In the following days, she had cause to discover plenty of both within her. After the incident with the hound, she knew she must go far away from people and dogs. And she knew what kinds of creatures dined on grubs, too. She slept out of sight under leaves, in places where grubs would not likely be sought.<BR><BR>
Even so, Einlea's days were filled with terror and adventure. There were circling hawks by day and owls by night. A bear, tearing at a rotting tree trunk, gobbled grubs, indistinguishable from Einlea, by the hundreds, as she watched in horror from behind a nearby rock. The smallest stream was now an enormous, gushing torrent, to be crossed in a nutshell under the greatest of peril. Einlea passed these tests, along with many others, and she passed them well.<BR><BR>
It was on her tenth such day that a clumsy boot kicked aside the piece of bark under which she had sought shelter from the sun. Blinded by the sudden light, she heard an exclamation from high above. Then, before she could react, two fingers dropped from the sky and plucked her up and deposited her firmly inside a huge fist.<BR><BR>
Ten days ago, Einlea would have been paralysed with terror. But that was ten days ago. Her mind raced. "Who is this clumsy idiot, anyway??" she thought, "and what on earth does he want with a tree grub? At least he didn't squash me on the spot. That's encouraging, isn't it? So he must be here to rescue me.."<BR><BR>
She wriggled and squirmed in his fist until she could see his face, high above her, between two of his fingers. "Ugh. A beard. If I'm going to be rescued, why can't it be by a fine young prince?" But it then occurred to her that she was speaking from old habit. "I wonder how many of those foppish boys could have survived these past ten days?" She laughed, thinking of them. "Not many, I bet. Those who wouldn't have curled up and died immediately would, by now, be whimpering and crying for their mothers." She looked at Kieran again. "Well ... maybe he would look better if I wasn't looking straight up his nostrils. Ouch.. Why isn't he more careful with me??"<BR><BR>
And then it occurred to Einlea that, if this oaf were truly rescuing her, he probably would have said something to her.<BR><BR>
"Uh-oh." Einlea's heart raced and she started wriggling furiously , imagining the worst of all possible deaths. "He must be going fishing."<BR><BR>
Einlea couldn't do much in her current state, but she could spit. And spit she did. In quantities unimaginable for so small a grub. She spit and spit and spit until her tiny grub mouth was too dry to spit another drop. She felt Kieran's hand squirming and thought, "It's working.."<BR><BR><BR><BR>
IV.<BR><BR>
Kieran was fair disgusted. Twas bad enough that he had to touch the slimy thing, but now it was oozing something and becoming truly revolting. Finally, just before he reached the robin's oak, he could take it no longer. He stopped and examined the creature in his hand. White and plump and glistening, it was, in truth, a repellent creature. Yet the poor thing was obviously terrified. It gazed up at him with what he imagined to be minuscule grub eyes, pleading. Kieran thought of the caterpillar and the earthworm, and his heart gave in. Heaving a great resigned sigh, he found a nice clean root and placed the grub upon it.<BR><BR>
And thus was Loziard's spell broken.<BR><BR>
None could have been more astonished than Einlea when she unexpectedly grew to her former size, except, perhaps for Kieran, who nearly died of fright. He was no more than catching his breath when Einlea regained her wits. Raising her index finger, warning Kieran not to say even ONE word, Einlea snatched Kieran's coat to cover herself. Then, with fire in her eyes, and as much dignity as she could muster, she was off to Trowbridge, leaving Kieran to stare, open-mouthed, at her departing figure.<BR><BR>
Einlea knew she could not simply enter the city and confront Loziard. The moment he saw her, he would but cast another enchantment upon her. So, disguising herself as a shepherd, she found an abandoned house on the moors and began to make her plans. What happened next is a tale worth hearing. But it is a tale for another evening. Indeed, it is a tale to be told over many an evening, and many a good pot of ale.<BR><BR>
And what of the baby robins? Having no alternative, Kieran climbed the tree and took from his pack his last piece of fatty mutton. Tearing it into small shreds, he gave it to the grateful mother robin, who fed it to her family.<BR><BR>
Upon returning to the ground, Kieran looked first toward Fairtree, his former destination, then, grinning, set off after the most surprising young lady, for whom he now had many questions. "Who knows ..." he called back to the robins, "It may be fate. And besides, I need my coat."<BR><BR>
He was heard, late that evening, far down the road, singing:<BR><BR>
"Oh, the maidens of Trowbridge are passing fair ...<BR><BR>
...with breasts like melons, and flaxen hair ..."<BR>"""
"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
基兰故事集<BR>
维杰皮西库斯 编辑<BR><BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
[图书馆员注......<BR><BR>
记录在案的吟游诗人基兰的故事分为三类：林地纪事、城堡与国王，以及一个未命名的淫秽故事系列（最近因神秘事故被毁）。有些是吟游诗人亲笔所写，而另一些仅仅是原作的影子，仅作为孩子们的睡前故事流传。其结构体现了听众在漫长冬夜围炉时偏爱的螺旋形式。至于它们是描述了真实事件，是寓言，还是仅仅是娱乐幻想，读者需自行判断。]<BR><BR><BR>
一、<BR><BR>
基兰走在从雷恩到费尔树的路上，被正午的太阳晒得疲惫不堪。他的靴子很紧，他想到附近一棵橡树的阴凉下脱掉它们（橡树是吟游诗人的最爱）。这棵橡树古老而多节，粗壮的树枝低垂摇摆，有些地方几乎触到地面。基兰在树荫下看着森林里的生物在温暖的阳光下嬉戏。除了头顶高处的树叶沙沙声，只有蝴蝶翅膀和鸟鸣声。<BR><BR>
“多么宁静的一天，”基兰看着一只蝴蝶飘过想道，“多么美好的一天！说实话，自从吟游诗人开始讲故事以来，还有比这更宁静、更美好的一天吗？”<BR><BR>
他喝了口水袋里的水，从袋子里拿出鲁特琴，清了清嗓子，开始唱道：<BR><BR>
“哦，雷恩的少女们美丽绝伦......<BR><BR>
......胸如蜜瓜，发似金丝......”<BR><BR>
他刚深吸一口气准备吼出那充满活力的副歌时，一个细小的女声说道：“好心的先生......”<BR><BR>
他穿着袜子跳了起来，脸涨得通红。“谁在那里？”他喊道。<BR><BR>
那个细小的声音重复道：“拜托了，先生，如果你愿意好心的话......”<BR><BR>
基兰环顾四周，却没有看到任何人或生物在跟他说话。<BR><BR>
“求你了，”他喊道。“现身吧，否则休怪我匕首无情。”（他拼命想自己最后一次见到它是在哪里。）“无论你是敌是友，求你现在就现身。”<BR><BR>
那个细小的声音从他上方回答道：“好心的先生，你没有理由怕我，我需要帮助。你能发发善心帮我吗？”<BR><BR>
他抬头望去，只在他上方三根树枝处看到一个小小知更鸟巢。他迅速爬上去，发现一只知更鸟和三只小小的雏鸟，它们嘴巴张得大大的。<BR><BR>
“好心的知更鸟妈妈，”他问道，“是你这样对我说话吗？”<BR><BR>
“好心的先生，”她回答说，“我的翅膀受伤了，至少需要一天才能飞。如果我的孩子们不快点吃东西，他们会死的。你能好心带点肥美多汁的食物来吗？你能为我的孩子们找条毛毛虫、蚯蚓或蛆虫吗？”<BR><BR>
基兰心地善良，无法拒绝这样的恳求，于是他走进了森林。他在一些桑叶下搜寻，很快发现了一条小小的绿色毛毛虫。这似乎是幼年知更鸟的完美食物。<BR><BR>
他把它从它正在进食的叶子上摘下来，准备赶紧回到橡树那里，这时他听到了一个细小的声音。他张开手，毛毛虫用她那双充满恐惧的棕色大眼睛抬头看着他。“好心的先生，”她说，“你会如此轻率地杀死我吗？”<BR><BR>
基兰困惑地挠了挠头，毛毛虫继续说道：“当你在橡树下凉脚时，难道你没有从我父母在阳光下在你面前跳舞的美丽中找到快乐吗？我也很快就要蜕变。你会剥夺你的后继者看我跳舞的快乐吗？如果我不能活着生孩子，你自己的孩子们又如何能找到这样的快乐？求你了，先生，蚯蚓难道就不能满足那些雏鸟的需要吗？<BR><BR>
基兰看着毛毛虫的眼睛，知道他不能把她喂给知更鸟。他小心地把她放在她的桑树下，继续寻找。<BR><BR>
在一条湍急的小溪附近，基兰找到一块扁平的石头，搬开后，露出一条肥美的蚯蚓正在享受凉爽湿润的泥土。“啊哈，”他想，“毛毛虫虽然不错，但这看起来确实更适合做小知更鸟的食物。”<BR><BR>
他刚把蚯蚓从它凉爽的住所（它一直在疯狂地试图挖洞躲避他）中拽出来，就听到了一个微弱得像是他想象出来的声音：<BR><BR>
“好心的先生，”他以为自己听到了，基兰看着自己的手。蚯蚓继续说：“我只是一个卑微的生物，这是真的，但我能否恳求一下呢？”<BR><BR>
基兰翻了个白眼，蚯蚓坐起来抓住了机会。“我不是你可能找到的其他那种低贱的蠕虫。不，我是蚯蚓中的王子。我来自一个古老的世系。当火焰从这片土地上的黑坑中喷出时，我的祖先在地下挖洞。我指挥着数百万像我一样的同类。如果没有我忠实的追随者，你，好心的先生，早就被树叶、树干和腐烂的尸体埋到脖子了。我要和你做个交易。如果你放了我，而是为那些雏鸟选一条可怜的蛆虫，我将派遣整个蚯蚓家族，在你活着的时候，让你的前院保持干净、气味清新。”蚯蚓满怀希望地看着基兰（同时计算着到地面的距离）。“好心的先生，你觉得如何？”<BR><BR>
基兰开始失去耐心，但考虑到蚯蚓提议的价值，他决定，一条蛆虫确实可以成为小知更鸟的美味。他把蚯蚓放回它潮湿的避难所，小心地盖上了上面的扁石头。果然，不久之后，在一片林间空地上，在一块宽大的废弃树皮下，基兰偶然发现了他要找的东西：一条肥硕的白色蛆虫，它将把雏鸟养成美丽的歌者。他把它从藏身处拽出来，出发了。这确实是美好的一天。<BR><BR><BR>
二、<BR><BR>
附近，在庄严的特罗布里奇，住着卡拉丹国王和他可爱的女儿艾恩莉娅。公主是老人眼中的掌上明珠，是他小小王国的王冠宝石。他以溺爱父亲的盲目自豪看着她，而她呢，只是在他的恩赐下茁壮成长，享受着一切。<BR><BR>
特罗布里奇现在很安静，主要的声音是马车轮子的咔哒声和街头小贩的叫卖声，但并非一直如此。三年前，与西边的卡森发生了麻烦。不是什么大事，只是一场边界争端，但国王说服了一位名叫洛齐亚德的巫师来特罗布里奇为他效力，帮助他应对争端。特罗布里奇没人认识洛齐亚德，他在宫殿里独来独往，随心所欲地进出。当特罗布里奇几乎不费一兵一卒就获胜时，随后进行了数天数周的欢乐庆祝。时间流逝，但洛齐亚德却留了下来。国王不想显得忘恩负义，什么也没说，但对巫师的存在越来越感到不安，希望他离开。<BR><BR>
在艾恩莉娅二十岁生日那天，卡拉丹国王下令在他的整个王国举行庆祝和放假。他的臣民们不知道，他打算宣布退位，并将王冠传给他美丽的女儿。仅仅是出于礼貌，他邀请了巫师洛齐亚德来帮他拟定一篇合适的演讲稿。<BR><BR>
洛齐亚德勃然大怒。他在房间里踱步，黑色的眉毛紧锁，那强烈的程度足以让任何牛奶变酸。“为什么，”他大声喊道，“那个老丑角如此不公正地对待我？如果不是我的技能，边界争端，甚至可能整个王国，都可能已经丢失了。我应得更多。我应得王冠。把它给他那个矫揉造作、傻笑、只想着自己任性的女儿，比手套的拍打还要刺痛。我要讨回公道。我要充分展示，让所有人看看，真正的权力在哪里。”<BR><BR>
于是，洛齐亚德开始做准备。<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅公主的生日在一个夏天的早晨到来。城里和城外农场的每个人都聚集到宫殿参加庆典。每个屋顶上都飘扬着旗帜。提琴手拉着琴，舞者跳着舞。面包师为此烘焙了美味的甜点。这是值得长久铭记的一天。<BR><BR>
正午时分，卡拉丹国王和艾恩莉娅公主在王国的欢呼声中出现在主阳台上。“特罗布里奇的好公民们，”国王喊道，“我们只是一个小小的王国，但我们繁荣昌盛，不是吗？”<BR><BR>
下面的人群中响起了（大多是）大声的欢呼。受到鼓舞，卡拉丹继续说道：“但现在我已经老了。年轻一代能更好地处理王国需求和事务的日子已经到来。我的臣民们......我忠诚的臣民和朋友们......我怀着荣誉......自豪......以及最大的期望......将我的王国和王权移交给我的爱女。我向大家宣布”（此处长停顿）“艾恩莉娅。”<BR><BR>
欢呼声响彻云霄，卡拉丹用胳膊做了一个宏大而横扫一切的手势，意图让这个交接仪式像充满他的自豪一样壮观。他的袍子“嗖”的一声，他的手却指向......空无一人。这是怎么回事？她去哪儿了？片刻前艾恩莉娅所在的地方，现在只有空荡荡的空气。<BR><BR>
“呃......艾恩莉娅......？”他不确定地喊道。但没有回应。公园和庭院陷入一片寂静。人们紧张地互相瞥了一眼。<BR><BR>
老洛齐亚德高兴地拍手。他跳起舞来。他无法抑制地大笑，抱住了自己。“多么美妙......”他喊道。“我是一个多么令人惊叹、才华横溢的巫师啊。”当然，他做的事，就是彻底摆脱了艾恩莉娅。他用狡猾而邪恶的一击，将这个虚荣的生物从宫殿中移除了。他和他的渴望之间，再无他物。<BR><BR>
魔法是件棘手的事。像世界上所有的力量一样，它必须保持平衡。正如白昼平衡黑夜，夏天平衡冬天一样，积极的魔法也必然平衡消极的魔法。每一个有害或破坏性的法术，都必须有一个同等善意或慈善的行为，以免麻烦泛滥到世界上。每一个黑巫师，都必须有一个白巫师。每一个战斗破坏法术，都必须有治疗。你要知道......如果所有练习魔法的人只施放治疗或保护法术，黑暗可怕的力量就会积聚，直到混乱和毁灭爆发，将我们的厄运倾泻而下。因此，治疗法术可能被伤害打破，而最恶毒的法术也可能被慈善打破。<BR><BR>
知道这一点，洛齐亚德精心策划了他的复仇行动。为了永久地摆脱艾恩莉娅（除了直接杀死她），他必须设计一个巧妙的法术，没有任何善行能打破它。一天深夜，他正从长胡子里捉虱子，突然大笑起来。他要把她变成某种......恶心的东西。<BR><BR>
“我要把她变成青蛙。”他笑了，然后皱起了眉头。不......那已经有人做过了。人们可能会预料到，像没脑子的白痴一样到处找青蛙，希望能赚到国王的赎金。<BR><BR>
然后，他想到了一个绝妙的计划。<BR><BR>
“我要把她变成一只虫子，一只昆虫，一条蠕虫......”他差点被酒呛到。“哦。多么完美啊......我要把她变成一种真正令人厌恶的东西，让她在她短暂的虫子生命中，始终活在恐惧中，害怕被第一个看到她的人踩扁。”他尖叫着，戒指叮当作响，肥肉颤抖着，笑着把酒从鼻子里喷了出来。“哦，真是太美味了......”<BR><BR>
他正是这么做的。当卡拉丹国王和他的臣民们困惑地挠头时，没人注意到一条肥硕的白色树蛆啪嗒一声掉在主阳台下的鹅卵石上，立刻蜷缩起来，闪闪发光，瑟瑟发抖。<BR><BR><BR>
三、<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅吓坏了。发生了什么？嗯，她见过洛齐亚德的魔法，足以知道发生了什么。但为什么？他为什么要这样对她？她没有太多时间思考这个问题。一只巨大的黑色猎犬，比她大数百倍，跑到她躺着的鹅卵石上，差点用舌头一口把她吞掉。她不知从哪儿找到了力气，滚出了它的路径，滚进了石缝之间。它那巨大、湿哒哒的舌头跟着她，滴着口水，喘着粗气，向她喷出炽热可怕的飓风。但就在舌头快要将她舔进等待的胃里时，猎犬的主人猛地一拉它的粗链子，把那畜生拉向了家的方向。<BR><BR>
确实，艾恩莉娅在她作为人类的生活中，是自我放纵的，不倾向于努力或机灵，但那仅仅是因为她不需要这两者。在接下来的日子里，她有理由发现自己内心有丰富的努力和机灵。经历了猎犬事件后，她知道必须远离人和狗。她也知道什么样的生物以蛆虫为食。她睡在树叶下看不见的地方，在那些不太可能被找到蛆虫的地方。<BR><BR>
即便如此，艾恩莉娅的日子也充满了恐惧和冒险。白天有盘旋的鹰，夜晚有猫头鹰。一只熊撕开一根腐烂的树干，成百上千地吞食着与艾恩莉娅无法区分的蛆虫，她惊恐地从附近一块岩石后面看着。最小的溪流现在也成了巨大汹涌的激流，必须冒着极大的危险才能渡过。艾恩莉娅通过了这些考验，还有许多其他的，而且她应对得很好。<BR><BR>
在她这样度过的第十天，一只笨拙的靴子踢开了她用来躲避阳光的那块树皮。突如其来的光线让她眼花缭乱，她听到高处传来一声惊呼。然后，还没等她反应过来，两根手指从天而降，将她抓起，稳稳地塞进了一个巨大的拳头里。<BR><BR>
十天前，艾恩莉娅会吓得瘫痪。但那是十天前的事了。她的思绪飞速运转。“这个笨手笨脚的白痴到底是谁？”她想，“他到底要一条树蛆做什么？至少他没有当场把我压扁。这很鼓舞人心，不是吗？所以他一定是来救我的......”<BR><BR>
她在他的拳头里扭动挣扎，直到她能透过他的两根手指之间看到他高高在上方的脸。“呃。有胡子。如果要被救，为什么不能是个英俊的年轻王子呢？”但她随即想到，自己这是出于旧习惯。“我想知道，那些浮夸的男孩中有多少能挺过这过去的十天？”她想着他们，笑了起来。“我打赌不多。那些没有立即蜷缩起来死掉的，现在大概也在抽泣着喊妈妈了。”她再次看向基兰。“嗯......如果我不是直接看着他的鼻孔，也许他会更好看一点。哎哟......他为什么不能对我更小心点？？”<BR><BR>
然后艾恩莉娅想到，如果这个蠢汉真的是来救她的，他大概会对她说点什么。<BR><BR>
“呃-哦。”艾恩莉娅的心狂跳起来，她开始拼命扭动，想象着所有可能的最糟糕的死法。“他一定是去钓鱼。”<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅在目前的状态下做不了太多，但她能吐口水。她吐了。吐出的量对于这么小的一条蛆来说难以想象。她吐了又吐，直到她那小小的蛆嘴干得再也吐不出一滴水。她感觉到基兰的手在蠕动，心想：“起作用了......”<BR><BR><BR><BR>
四、<BR><BR>
基兰相当厌恶。他不得不触碰那黏糊糊的东西已经够糟了，可现在它还在渗出某种东西，变得真正令人作呕。终于，在他快要到达知更鸟橡树时，他再也无法忍受了。他停下来，仔细检查手中的生物。白色、肥硕、闪闪发光，说实话，这是一种令人排斥的生物。但这可怜的小东西显然吓坏了。它用它那在他看来是微小蛆眼的眼睛抬头看着他，仿佛在恳求。基兰想起了毛毛虫和蚯蚓，他的心软了。他无奈地长叹一口气，找了一条干净的好树根，把蛆虫放了上去。<BR><BR>
就这样，洛齐亚德的法术被打破了。<BR><BR>
当艾恩莉娅意外地恢复到她原来的大小时，没有人比她更惊讶了，也许除了基兰，他差点吓死。他还没喘过气来，艾恩莉娅就恢复了神智。她竖起食指，警告基兰一个字也不要说，然后一把抓过基兰的外套遮住自己。接着，她眼中燃烧着怒火，尽其所能地保持着尊严，向特罗布里奇走去，留下基兰目瞪口呆地望着她离去的身影。<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅知道她不能直接进城去面对洛齐亚德。他一看到她，只会对她施另一个魔法。于是，她把自己伪装成牧羊人，在荒原上找到一栋废弃的房子，开始制定计划。接下来发生的事是个值得一听的故事。但那是个改天再讲的故事。确实，那是一个需要花许多个晚上，就着许多壶好麦酒才能讲完的故事。<BR><BR>
那些小知更鸟呢？基兰别无选择，爬上树，从背包里拿出他最后一块肥羊肉。他把肉撕成小碎片，给了感激的知更鸟妈妈，她喂给了她的家人。<BR><BR>
回到地面后，基兰先看了看他原本的目的地费尔树，然后咧嘴一笑，朝着那位最令人惊讶的年轻女士追去，他现在对她有很多疑问。“谁知道呢......”他回头对知更鸟喊道，“也许是命运吧。再说了，我需要我的外套。”<BR><BR>
那天深夜，有人听到他在很远的路那头唱道：<BR><BR>
“哦，特罗布里奇的少女们美丽绝伦......<BR><BR>
......胸如蜜瓜，发似金丝......”<BR>"""

"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
Tales of Kieran<BR>
Vegepythicus, editor<BR><BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
[Librarian's Note ...<BR><BR>
The recorded tales of Kieran the Bard fall into three categories: the Woodland Cycle, Castles and Kings, and an unnamed cycle of lusty tales (recently destroyed by mysterious accident). Some are in the bard's own hand, while others, mere shadows of the originals, remain only as bedtime tales for children. The structure exemplifies the helical form favored by listeners about the hearth on a long winter's eve. As to whether they describe real events, be allegory, or be mere entertaining fancy, the reader must decide.]<BR><BR><BR>
I.<BR><BR>
Kieran was on the road from Wren to Fairtree, when he grew weary from the midday sun. His boots were tight and he thought to remove them for a bit in the shade of a nearby oak (oaks being a favorite of bards). This particular oak was venerable and gnarled, with sturdy branches that dipped and swooped, nearly touching the ground in spots. From its shade Kieran watched the forest creatures playing in the warm sun. But for the rustling of leaves, high above, the only sounds were of butterfly wings and birdsong.<BR><BR>
"What a peaceful day," Kieran thought as he watched a butterfly drift by, "What a beautiful day! In truth, since bards first told tales, has there ever been a day more peaceful and beautiful than this?"<BR><BR>
He drank from his waterskin and, taking his lute from its sack, cleared his throat and began to sing:<BR><BR>
"Oh, the maidens of Wren are passing fair ...<BR><BR>
...with breasts like melons, and flaxen hair ..."<BR><BR>
He had just taken a deep breath to bellow the lusty chorus when a small, feminine voice said, "Kind sir ..."<BR><BR>
He leaped to his stockinged feet, his face flaming red. "Who's there?" he cried.<BR><BR>
The small voice repeated, "Please, sir, if you will be so kind ..."<BR><BR>
Kieran looked about but saw no person or creature addressing him.<BR><BR>
"Pray thee," he cried. "Show thyself or have cause to fear my dagger." (He tried desperately to remember where he had last seen it.) "Whether thee be friend or foe, pray thee show thyself now."<BR><BR>
The small voice replied from above him, "Kind sir, thou hast no cause to fear me, and I am in need of help. Can thou find it in thy heart to aid me?"<BR><BR>
He looked up and saw naught but a small robin's nest, three branches above him. Climbing swiftly, he found a robin with three tiny robinlings, their mouths open wide.<BR><BR>
"Good mother robin," he asked, "Can it be thee who addresses me thus?"<BR><BR>
"Kind sir," she replied, "I have hurt my wing and it will be at least a day before I might fly. If my children do not eat soon, they will die. Would you be so kind as to bring a fat, juicy meal? Would you find a caterpillar or earthworm or grub for my children?"<BR><BR>
Now, Kieran was kind of heart and it was not within him to refuse a plea such as this, so off he went into the forest. Searching under some mulberry leaves, he soon found a small green caterpillar. It seemed a perfect meal for young robins.<BR><BR>
Plucking it from the leaf upon which it fed, he prepared to hurry back to the oak when he heard a tiny voice. He opened his hand and the caterpillar looked up at him with her big brown eyes wide with fear. "Kind sir," she said, "wouldst thou kill me so thoughtlessly?"<BR><BR>
Kieran scratched his head in puzzlement and the caterpillar continued: "When thou cooled thy feet beneath the oak, didst thou not find joy in my parents' beauty as they danced before thee in the sun? I, too, am soon to change. Wouldst thou deny thy successors the joy of my dancing? And if I do not live to have children, how will thine own children find such joy? Please, sir, would not an earthworm serve the needs of the robinlings just as well?<BR><BR>
Kieran looked into the eyes of the caterpillar and knew that he could not feed her to the robins. Carefully, he placed her beneath her mulberry bush and continued his search.<BR><BR>
Near a rushing brook, Kieran found a flat stone that, when moved, revealed a juicy earthworm enjoying the cool moist earth. "Aha." he thought. "As nice as the caterpillar may have been, this truly seems a more fitting meal for young robins."<BR><BR>
He had no sooner plucked the earthworm from it's cool abode (where it had been frantically trying to burrow away from him), when he heard a voice so faint he might have imagined it:<BR><BR>
"Kind sir," he thought he heard, and Kieran looked in his hand. The worm continued: "I am but a lowly creature, it's true, but might I plead such case that I have?"<BR><BR>
Kieran rolled his eyes skyward as the worm sat up and seized its chance. "I am not a lowborn worm like others you might find. No, I am a prince among earthworms. I come from an ancient lineage. My ancestors burrowed the earth when fires belched from black pits throughout these lands. I command millions like myself. Were it not for my loyal followers, you, good sir, would be up to your neck in leaves, tree trunks and mouldy carcasses. I'll make a bargain with you. If you release me and choose, instead, a pathetic grub for the robinlings, I will dispatch an entire clan of earthworms to keep your foreyard clean and sweet-smelling for as long as ye shall live." The earthworm looked hopefully at Kieran (while calculating the distance to the ground). "Good sir, what say ye?"<BR><BR>
Kieran was beginning to lose his patience, but, seeing the value of the earthworm's offer, decided that a grub would, indeed, make a tasty morsel for the young robins. He returned the earthworm to its moist haven and carefully replaced the flat stone above it. And, true to his desire, a short while later, in a forest glade, beneath a wide slab of discarded bark, Kieran chanced upon that which he sought: a fat white grub that would grow the robinlings into beautiful songsters. He plucked it from its hiding place and set forth. It was a beautiful day, indeed.<BR><BR><BR>
II.<BR><BR>
Nearby, in stately Trowbridge, King Caladan did live with his lovely daughter, Einlea. The princess was the apple of the old man's eye and the crown jewel of his small kingdom. He looked upon her with the blind pride of a doting father, and she, for her part, did naught but bask and flourish in his bounty.<BR><BR>
Trowbridge was quiet now, the chief sounds being the clatter of cart wheels and the cries of street vendors, but it was not always so. Three years earlier there had been trouble with Carthan to the west. It was not much, a border dispute, but the king persuaded a wizard named Loziard to come to Trowbridge in his employ, to aid him in the contest. Loziard was unknown by all in Trowbridge and kept to himself within the palace, coming and going as he pleased. When Trowbridge prevailed, with almost no loss of life, there was joyous celebration for days and weeks thereafter. Time passed, yet Loziard remained. The King, not wanting to seem ungrateful, said nothing, but became increasingly discomforted with the wizard's presence and wished for his departure.<BR><BR>
On Einlea's twentieth birthday, King Caladan called for a celebration and holiday through all his land. Unknown to his subjects, he intended to proclaim his retirement and the transference of his crown to his beautiful daughter. Out of politeness, and nothing more, he invited the wizard Loziard to aid him in devising a proper speech.<BR><BR>
Loziard was furious. He paced his chamber, his black brows knitted with intensity that would have soured any cow's milk. "Why," he cried aloud, "am I treated so unjustly by the old buffoon? Were it not for my skills, the border contest, mayhaps even the kingdom itself, might have been lost. I deserve more. I deserve the crown. To give it to that primping simpering daughter of his, who thinks naught of more than her own whim, is a slap more stinging than that of gauntlet. I will have justice. I will demonstrate, amply, for all to see, wherein lies true power."<BR><BR>
Thereupon, Loziard made his preparations.<BR><BR>
Princess Einlea's birthday came on a summer morning. Everyone within the city, and from the farms without, gathered to the palace for the festival. Banners waved from every rooftop. Fiddlers fiddled and dancers danced. Bakers baked wonderful sweets for the occasion. It was a day long to be remembered.<BR><BR>
At noon, precisely, King Caladan and Princess Einlea emerged onto the main balcony to the cheers of the kingdom. "Good citizens of Trowbridge," called the King, "We are but a tiny kingdom, but we prosper, do we not?"<BR><BR>
Loud hails (mostly) erupted from the crowd below. Encouraged, Caladan continued, "But now I am an old man. The day has arrived when younger blood can better attend to the needs and events of the kingdom. My subjects ... My loyal subjects and friends ... It is with honor ...and pride ...and the greatest of expectations ...that I transfer my kingdom and my crown to my loving daughter. To one and all, I give you" (a long pause here) "Einlea."<BR><BR>
As cheers filled the air, Caladan made a grand, sweeping gesture with his arm, intending to make the presentation as spectacular as the pride that filled him. His robe went "swoooosh" and his hand pointed to ... nobody. What was this? Where had she gone? Where Einlea had been, moments earlier, there now was naught but vacant air.<BR><BR>
"Er ...Einlea ...?" he called, uncertainly. But there was no response. Silence fell over park and courtyard. People glanced at each other nervously.<BR><BR>
Old Loziard clapped his hands in glee. He danced. He hugged himself with uncontained laughter. "How wonderful ..." he cried. "What a breathtakingly stunning and talented a wizard I am.." For what he had done, of course, was to rid himself of Einlea for once and for all. With one stroke, crafty and evil, he had removed the vain creature from the palace. Nought else remained between him and that which he desired.<BR><BR>
Now, magic is a tricky thing. Like all forces in the world, it must be kept in balance. As surely as day balances night and summer balances winter, so too must positive magic balance negative. For every hurtful or destructive spell, there must be an act of equal goodness or charity lest trouble overflow into the world. For every black wizard, there must be a white. For every spell of combat destruction, there must be healing. Know ye this ...if all who practice magic cast naught but healing or protective spells, dark, horrible forces would build up until chaos and ruin would burst forth and rain our doom down upon us. Thus may spells of healing be broken by harm, and the worst of spells be broken by charity.<BR><BR>
Knowing this, Loziard planned well his act of vengeance. To permanently rid himself of Einlea (short of killing her outright) he must devise a spell so cunning that no act of kindness would ever break it. He was pulling lice out of his long beard, late one evening, when he burst into laughter. He would make her into something ...disgusting.<BR><BR>
"I will make her into a frog." he laughed, then frowned. No ... that had been done. People might expect it and go around, like mindless idiots, seeking frogs, hoping to earn a kings ransom.<BR><BR>
And then, a brilliant plan occurred to him.<BR><BR>
"I will make her into a bug, an insect, a WORM ..." He almost choked on his wine. "Oh. How perfect.. I will make her into something so truly loathsome that she will spend the rest of her little bug life in terror of being squashed by the first person who sees her." He squealed and his rings jangled and his fat jiggled and he snorted wine out his nose in laughter. "Oh, how absolutely delicious ..."<BR><BR>
And that's exactly what he did. While King Caladan and his subjects scratched their heads in puzzlement, nobody saw a small fat white tree grub plop to the cobblestones beneath the main balcony and immediately curl up, glistening and quivering.<BR><BR><BR>
III.<BR><BR>
Einlea was terrified. What had happened? Well, she had seen enough of Loziard's magic to know what had happened. But why? Why would he do this to her? She didn't have long to ponder the question. A huge black hound, hundreds of times her size, ran to the cobblestone where she lay, and almost gobbled her with one slurp of his tongue. From somewhere, she found the wherewithal to roll out of his way and into the crevice between the stones. His HUGE slurpy tongue followed her, drooling and panting great hurricanes of hot awful breath down at her. But just as the tongue was about to lick her into the waiting stomach, the hound's owner yanked his massive chain and pulled the beast toward home.<BR><BR>
It is true that Einlea, in her life as a human, was self indulgent and not inclined to effort or resource, but that was merely because she had no need of either. In the following days, she had cause to discover plenty of both within her. After the incident with the hound, she knew she must go far away from people and dogs. And she knew what kinds of creatures dined on grubs, too. She slept out of sight under leaves, in places where grubs would not likely be sought.<BR><BR>
Even so, Einlea's days were filled with terror and adventure. There were circling hawks by day and owls by night. A bear, tearing at a rotting tree trunk, gobbled grubs, indistinguishable from Einlea, by the hundreds, as she watched in horror from behind a nearby rock. The smallest stream was now an enormous, gushing torrent, to be crossed in a nutshell under the greatest of peril. Einlea passed these tests, along with many others, and she passed them well.<BR><BR>
It was on her tenth such day that a clumsy boot kicked aside the piece of bark under which she had sought shelter from the sun. Blinded by the sudden light, she heard an exclamation from high above. Then, before she could react, two fingers dropped from the sky and plucked her up and deposited her firmly inside a huge fist.<BR><BR>
Ten days ago, Einlea would have been paralysed with terror. But that was ten days ago. Her mind raced. "Who is this clumsy idiot, anyway??" she thought, "and what on earth does he want with a tree grub? At least he didn't squash me on the spot. That's encouraging, isn't it? So he must be here to rescue me.."<BR><BR>
She wriggled and squirmed in his fist until she could see his face, high above her, between two of his fingers. "Ugh. A beard. If I'm going to be rescued, why can't it be by a fine young prince?" But it then occurred to her that she was speaking from old habit. "I wonder how many of those foppish boys could have survived these past ten days?" She laughed, thinking of them. "Not many, I bet. Those who wouldn't have curled up and died immediately would, by now, be whimpering and crying for their mothers." She looked at Kieran again. "Well ... maybe he would look better if I wasn't looking straight up his nostrils. Ouch.. Why isn't he more careful with me??"<BR><BR>
And then it occurred to Einlea that, if this oaf were truly rescuing her, he probably would have said something to her.<BR><BR>
"Uh-oh." Einlea's heart raced and she started wriggling furiously , imagining the worst of all possible deaths. "He must be going fishing."<BR><BR>
Einlea couldn't do much in her current state, but she could spit. And spit she did. In quantities unimaginable for so small a grub. She spit and spit and spit until her tiny grub mouth was too dry to spit another drop. She felt Kieran's hand squirming and thought, "It's working.."<BR><BR><BR><BR>
IV.<BR><BR>
Kieran was fair disgusted. Twas bad enough that he had to touch the slimy thing, but now it was oozing something and becoming truly revolting. Finally, just before he reached the robin's oak, he could take it no longer. He stopped and examined the creature in his hand. White and plump and glistening, it was, in truth, a repellent creature. Yet the poor thing was obviously terrified. It gazed up at him with what he imagined to be minuscule grub eyes, pleading. Kieran thought of the caterpillar and the earthworm, and his heart gave in. Heaving a great resigned sigh, he found a nice clean root and placed the grub upon it.<BR><BR>
And thus was Loziard's spell broken.<BR><BR>
None could have been more astonished than Einlea when she unexpectedly grew to her former size, except, perhaps for Kieran, who nearly died of fright. He was no more than catching his breath when Einlea regained her wits. Raising her index finger, warning Kieran not to say even ONE word, Einlea snatched Kieran's coat to cover herself. Then, with fire in her eyes, and as much dignity as she could muster, she was off to Trowbridge, leaving Kieran to stare, open-mouthed, at her departing figure.<BR><BR>
Einlea knew she could not simply enter the city and confront Loziard. The moment he saw her, he would but cast another enchantment upon her. So, disguising herself as a shepherd, she found an abandoned house on the moors and began to make her plans. What happened next is a tale worth hearing. But it is a tale for another evening. Indeed, it is a tale to be told over many an evening, and many a good pot of ale.<BR><BR>
And what of the baby robins? Having no alternative, Kieran climbed the tree and took from his pack his last piece of fatty mutton. Tearing it into small shreds, he gave it to the grateful mother robin, who fed it to her family.<BR><BR>
Upon returning to the ground, Kieran looked first toward Fairtree, his former destination, then, grinning, set off after the most surprising young lady, for whom he now had many questions. "Who knows ..." he called back to the robins, "It may be fate. And besides, I need my coat."<BR><BR>
He was heard, late that evening, far down the road, singing:<BR><BR>
"Oh, the maidens of Trowbridge are passing fair ...<BR><BR>
...with breasts like melons, and flaxen hair ..."<BR>"""
"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
基兰故事集<BR>
维杰皮西库斯 编辑<BR><BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
[图书馆员注......<BR><BR>
记录在案的吟游诗人基兰的故事分为三类：林地纪事、城堡与国王，以及一个未命名的淫秽故事系列（最近因神秘事故被毁）。有些是吟游诗人亲笔所写，而另一些仅仅是原作的影子，仅作为孩子们的睡前故事流传。其结构体现了听众在漫长冬夜围炉时偏爱的螺旋形式。至于它们是描述了真实事件，是寓言，还是仅仅是娱乐幻想，读者需自行判断。]<BR><BR><BR>
一、<BR><BR>
基兰走在从雷恩到费尔树的路上，被正午的太阳晒得疲惫不堪。他的靴子很紧，他想到附近一棵橡树的阴凉下脱掉它们（橡树是吟游诗人的最爱）。这棵橡树古老而多节，粗壮的树枝低垂摇摆，有些地方几乎触到地面。基兰在树荫下看着森林里的生物在温暖的阳光下嬉戏。除了头顶高处的树叶沙沙声，只有蝴蝶翅膀和鸟鸣声。<BR><BR>
“多么宁静的一天，”基兰看着一只蝴蝶飘过想道，“多么美好的一天！说实话，自从吟游诗人开始讲故事以来，还有比这更宁静、更美好的一天吗？”<BR><BR>
他喝了口水袋里的水，从袋子里拿出鲁特琴，清了清嗓子，开始唱道：<BR><BR>
“哦，雷恩的少女们美丽绝伦......<BR><BR>
......胸如蜜瓜，发似金丝......”<BR><BR>
他刚深吸一口气准备吼出那充满活力的副歌时，一个细小的女声说道：“好心的先生......”<BR><BR>
他穿着袜子跳了起来，脸涨得通红。“谁在那里？”他喊道。<BR><BR>
那个细小的声音重复道：“拜托了，先生，如果你愿意好心的话......”<BR><BR>
基兰环顾四周，却没有看到任何人或生物在跟他说话。<BR><BR>
“求你了，”他喊道。“现身吧，否则休怪我匕首无情。”（他拼命想自己最后一次见到它是在哪里。）“无论你是敌是友，求你现在就现身。”<BR><BR>
那个细小的声音从他上方回答道：“好心的先生，你没有理由怕我，我需要帮助。你能发发善心帮我吗？”<BR><BR>
他抬头望去，只在他上方三根树枝处看到一个小小知更鸟巢。他迅速爬上去，发现一只知更鸟和三只小小的雏鸟，它们嘴巴张得大大的。<BR><BR>
“好心的知更鸟妈妈，”他问道，“是你这样对我说话吗？”<BR><BR>
“好心的先生，”她回答说，“我的翅膀受伤了，至少需要一天才能飞。如果我的孩子们不快点吃东西，他们会死的。你能好心带点肥美多汁的食物来吗？你能为我的孩子们找条毛毛虫、蚯蚓或蛆虫吗？”<BR><BR>
基兰心地善良，无法拒绝这样的恳求，于是他走进了森林。他在一些桑叶下搜寻，很快发现了一条小小的绿色毛毛虫。这似乎是幼年知更鸟的完美食物。<BR><BR>
他把它从它正在进食的叶子上摘下来，准备赶紧回到橡树那里，这时他听到了一个细小的声音。他张开手，毛毛虫用她那双充满恐惧的棕色大眼睛抬头看着他。“好心的先生，”她说，“你会如此轻率地杀死我吗？”<BR><BR>
基兰困惑地挠了挠头，毛毛虫继续说道：“当你在橡树下凉脚时，难道你没有从我父母在阳光下在你面前跳舞的美丽中找到快乐吗？我也很快就要蜕变。你会剥夺你的后继者看我跳舞的快乐吗？如果我不能活着生孩子，你自己的孩子们又如何能找到这样的快乐？求你了，先生，蚯蚓难道就不能满足那些雏鸟的需要吗？<BR><BR>
基兰看着毛毛虫的眼睛，知道他不能把她喂给知更鸟。他小心地把她放在她的桑树下，继续寻找。<BR><BR>
在一条湍急的小溪附近，基兰找到一块扁平的石头，搬开后，露出一条肥美的蚯蚓正在享受凉爽湿润的泥土。“啊哈，”他想，“毛毛虫虽然不错，但这看起来确实更适合做小知更鸟的食物。”<BR><BR>
他刚把蚯蚓从它凉爽的住所（它一直在疯狂地试图挖洞躲避他）中拽出来，就听到了一个微弱得像是他想象出来的声音：<BR><BR>
“好心的先生，”他以为自己听到了，基兰看着自己的手。蚯蚓继续说：“我只是一个卑微的生物，这是真的，但我能否恳求一下呢？”<BR><BR>
基兰翻了个白眼，蚯蚓坐起来抓住了机会。“我不是你可能找到的其他那种低贱的蠕虫。不，我是蚯蚓中的王子。我来自一个古老的世系。当火焰从这片土地上的黑坑中喷出时，我的祖先在地下挖洞。我指挥着数百万像我一样的同类。如果没有我忠实的追随者，你，好心的先生，早就被树叶、树干和腐烂的尸体埋到脖子了。我要和你做个交易。如果你放了我，而是为那些雏鸟选一条可怜的蛆虫，我将派遣整个蚯蚓家族，在你活着的时候，让你的前院保持干净、气味清新。”蚯蚓满怀希望地看着基兰（同时计算着到地面的距离）。“好心的先生，你觉得如何？”<BR><BR>
基兰开始失去耐心，但考虑到蚯蚓提议的价值，他决定，一条蛆虫确实可以成为小知更鸟的美味。他把蚯蚓放回它潮湿的避难所，小心地盖上了上面的扁石头。果然，不久之后，在一片林间空地上，在一块宽大的废弃树皮下，基兰偶然发现了他要找的东西：一条肥硕的白色蛆虫，它将把雏鸟养成美丽的歌者。他把它从藏身处拽出来，出发了。这确实是美好的一天。<BR><BR><BR>
二、<BR><BR>
附近，在庄严的特罗布里奇，住着卡拉丹国王和他可爱的女儿艾恩莉娅。公主是老人眼中的掌上明珠，是他小小王国的王冠宝石。他以溺爱父亲的盲目自豪看着她，而她呢，只是在他的恩赐下茁壮成长，享受着一切。<BR><BR>
特罗布里奇现在很安静，主要的声音是马车轮子的咔哒声和街头小贩的叫卖声，但并非一直如此。三年前，与西边的卡森发生了麻烦。不是什么大事，只是一场边界争端，但国王说服了一位名叫洛齐亚德的巫师来特罗布里奇为他效力，帮助他应对争端。特罗布里奇没人认识洛齐亚德，他在宫殿里独来独往，随心所欲地进出。当特罗布里奇几乎不费一兵一卒就获胜时，随后进行了数天数周的欢乐庆祝。时间流逝，但洛齐亚德却留了下来。国王不想显得忘恩负义，什么也没说，但对巫师的存在越来越感到不安，希望他离开。<BR><BR>
在艾恩莉娅二十岁生日那天，卡拉丹国王下令在他的整个王国举行庆祝和放假。他的臣民们不知道，他打算宣布退位，并将王冠传给他美丽的女儿。仅仅是出于礼貌，他邀请了巫师洛齐亚德来帮他拟定一篇合适的演讲稿。<BR><BR>
洛齐亚德勃然大怒。他在房间里踱步，黑色的眉毛紧锁，那强烈的程度足以让任何牛奶变酸。“为什么，”他大声喊道，“那个老丑角如此不公正地对待我？如果不是我的技能，边界争端，甚至可能整个王国，都可能已经丢失了。我应得更多。我应得王冠。把它给他那个矫揉造作、傻笑、只想着自己任性的女儿，比手套的拍打还要刺痛。我要讨回公道。我要充分展示，让所有人看看，真正的权力在哪里。”<BR><BR>
于是，洛齐亚德开始做准备。<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅公主的生日在一个夏天的早晨到来。城里和城外农场的每个人都聚集到宫殿参加庆典。每个屋顶上都飘扬着旗帜。提琴手拉着琴，舞者跳着舞。面包师为此烘焙了美味的甜点。这是值得长久铭记的一天。<BR><BR>
正午时分，卡拉丹国王和艾恩莉娅公主在王国的欢呼声中出现在主阳台上。“特罗布里奇的好公民们，”国王喊道，“我们只是一个小小的王国，但我们繁荣昌盛，不是吗？”<BR><BR>
下面的人群中响起了（大多是）大声的欢呼。受到鼓舞，卡拉丹继续说道：“但现在我已经老了。年轻一代能更好地处理王国需求和事务的日子已经到来。我的臣民们......我忠诚的臣民和朋友们......我怀着荣誉......自豪......以及最大的期望......将我的王国和王权移交给我的爱女。我向大家宣布”（此处长停顿）“艾恩莉娅。”<BR><BR>
欢呼声响彻云霄，卡拉丹用胳膊做了一个宏大而横扫一切的手势，意图让这个交接仪式像充满他的自豪一样壮观。他的袍子“嗖”的一声，他的手却指向......空无一人。这是怎么回事？她去哪儿了？片刻前艾恩莉娅所在的地方，现在只有空荡荡的空气。<BR><BR>
“呃......艾恩莉娅......？”他不确定地喊道。但没有回应。公园和庭院陷入一片寂静。人们紧张地互相瞥了一眼。<BR><BR>
老洛齐亚德高兴地拍手。他跳起舞来。他无法抑制地大笑，抱住了自己。“多么美妙......”他喊道。“我是一个多么令人惊叹、才华横溢的巫师啊。”当然，他做的事，就是彻底摆脱了艾恩莉娅。他用狡猾而邪恶的一击，将这个虚荣的生物从宫殿中移除了。他和他的渴望之间，再无他物。<BR><BR>
魔法是件棘手的事。像世界上所有的力量一样，它必须保持平衡。正如白昼平衡黑夜，夏天平衡冬天一样，积极的魔法也必然平衡消极的魔法。每一个有害或破坏性的法术，都必须有一个同等善意或慈善的行为，以免麻烦泛滥到世界上。每一个黑巫师，都必须有一个白巫师。每一个战斗破坏法术，都必须有治疗。你要知道......如果所有练习魔法的人只施放治疗或保护法术，黑暗可怕的力量就会积聚，直到混乱和毁灭爆发，将我们的厄运倾泻而下。因此，治疗法术可能被伤害打破，而最恶毒的法术也可能被慈善打破。<BR><BR>
知道这一点，洛齐亚德精心策划了他的复仇行动。为了永久地摆脱艾恩莉娅（除了直接杀死她），他必须设计一个巧妙的法术，没有任何善行能打破它。一天深夜，他正从长胡子里捉虱子，突然大笑起来。他要把她变成某种......恶心的东西。<BR><BR>
“我要把她变成青蛙。”他笑了，然后皱起了眉头。不......那已经有人做过了。人们可能会预料到，像没脑子的白痴一样到处找青蛙，希望能赚到国王的赎金。<BR><BR>
然后，他想到了一个绝妙的计划。<BR><BR>
“我要把她变成一只虫子，一只昆虫，一条蠕虫......”他差点被酒呛到。“哦。多么完美啊......我要把她变成一种真正令人厌恶的东西，让她在她短暂的虫子生命中，始终活在恐惧中，害怕被第一个看到她的人踩扁。”他尖叫着，戒指叮当作响，肥肉颤抖着，笑着把酒从鼻子里喷了出来。“哦，真是太美味了......”<BR><BR>
他正是这么做的。当卡拉丹国王和他的臣民们困惑地挠头时，没人注意到一条肥硕的白色树蛆啪嗒一声掉在主阳台下的鹅卵石上，立刻蜷缩起来，闪闪发光，瑟瑟发抖。<BR><BR><BR>
三、<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅吓坏了。发生了什么？嗯，她见过洛齐亚德的魔法，足以知道发生了什么。但为什么？他为什么要这样对她？她没有太多时间思考这个问题。一只巨大的黑色猎犬，比她大数百倍，跑到她躺着的鹅卵石上，差点用舌头一口把她吞掉。她不知从哪儿找到了力气，滚出了它的路径，滚进了石缝之间。它那巨大、湿哒哒的舌头跟着她，滴着口水，喘着粗气，向她喷出炽热可怕的飓风。但就在舌头快要将她舔进等待的胃里时，猎犬的主人猛地一拉它的粗链子，把那畜生拉向了家的方向。<BR><BR>
确实，艾恩莉娅在她作为人类的生活中，是自我放纵的，不倾向于努力或机灵，但那仅仅是因为她不需要这两者。在接下来的日子里，她有理由发现自己内心有丰富的努力和机灵。经历了猎犬事件后，她知道必须远离人和狗。她也知道什么样的生物以蛆虫为食。她睡在树叶下看不见的地方，在那些不太可能被找到蛆虫的地方。<BR><BR>
即便如此，艾恩莉娅的日子也充满了恐惧和冒险。白天有盘旋的鹰，夜晚有猫头鹰。一只熊撕开一根腐烂的树干，成百上千地吞食着与艾恩莉娅无法区分的蛆虫，她惊恐地从附近一块岩石后面看着。最小的溪流现在也成了巨大汹涌的激流，必须冒着极大的危险才能渡过。艾恩莉娅通过了这些考验，还有许多其他的，而且她应对得很好。<BR><BR>
在她这样度过的第十天，一只笨拙的靴子踢开了她用来躲避阳光的那块树皮。突如其来的光线让她眼花缭乱，她听到高处传来一声惊呼。然后，还没等她反应过来，两根手指从天而降，将她抓起，稳稳地塞进了一个巨大的拳头里。<BR><BR>
十天前，艾恩莉娅会吓得瘫痪。但那是十天前的事了。她的思绪飞速运转。“这个笨手笨脚的白痴到底是谁？”她想，“他到底要一条树蛆做什么？至少他没有当场把我压扁。这很鼓舞人心，不是吗？所以他一定是来救我的......”<BR><BR>
她在他的拳头里扭动挣扎，直到她能透过他的两根手指之间看到他高高在上方的脸。“呃。有胡子。如果要被救，为什么不能是个英俊的年轻王子呢？”但她随即想到，自己这是出于旧习惯。“我想知道，那些浮夸的男孩中有多少能挺过这过去的十天？”她想着他们，笑了起来。“我打赌不多。那些没有立即蜷缩起来死掉的，现在大概也在抽泣着喊妈妈了。”她再次看向基兰。“嗯......如果我不是直接看着他的鼻孔，也许他会更好看一点。哎哟......他为什么不能对我更小心点？？”<BR><BR>
然后艾恩莉娅想到，如果这个蠢汉真的是来救她的，他大概会对她说点什么。<BR><BR>
“呃-哦。”艾恩莉娅的心狂跳起来，她开始拼命扭动，想象着所有可能的最糟糕的死法。“他一定是去钓鱼。”<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅在目前的状态下做不了太多，但她能吐口水。她吐了。吐出的量对于这么小的一条蛆来说难以想象。她吐了又吐，直到她那小小的蛆嘴干得再也吐不出一滴水。她感觉到基兰的手在蠕动，心想：“起作用了......”<BR><BR><BR><BR>
四、<BR><BR>
基兰相当厌恶。他不得不触碰那黏糊糊的东西已经够糟了，可现在它还在渗出某种东西，变得真正令人作呕。终于，在他快要到达知更鸟橡树时，他再也无法忍受了。他停下来，仔细检查手中的生物。白色、肥硕、闪闪发光，说实话，这是一种令人排斥的生物。但这可怜的小东西显然吓坏了。它用它那在他看来是微小蛆眼的眼睛抬头看着他，仿佛在恳求。基兰想起了毛毛虫和蚯蚓，他的心软了。他无奈地长叹一口气，找了一条干净的好树根，把蛆虫放了上去。<BR><BR>
就这样，洛齐亚德的法术被打破了。<BR><BR>
当艾恩莉娅意外地恢复到她原来的大小时，没有人比她更惊讶了，也许除了基兰，他差点吓死。他还没喘过气来，艾恩莉娅就恢复了神智。她竖起食指，警告基兰一个字也不要说，然后一把抓过基兰的外套遮住自己。接着，她眼中燃烧着怒火，尽其所能地保持着尊严，向特罗布里奇走去，留下基兰目瞪口呆地望着她离去的身影。<BR><BR>
艾恩莉娅知道她不能直接进城去面对洛齐亚德。他一看到她，只会对她施另一个魔法。于是，她把自己伪装成牧羊人，在荒原上找到一栋废弃的房子，开始制定计划。接下来发生的事是个值得一听的故事。但那是个改天再讲的故事。确实，那是一个需要花许多个晚上，就着许多壶好麦酒才能讲完的故事。<BR><BR>
那些小知更鸟呢？基兰别无选择，爬上树，从背包里拿出他最后一块肥羊肉。他把肉撕成小碎片，给了感激的知更鸟妈妈，她喂给了她的家人。<BR><BR>
回到地面后，基兰先看了看他原本的目的地费尔树，然后咧嘴一笑，朝着那位最令人惊讶的年轻女士追去，他现在对她有很多疑问。“谁知道呢......”他回头对知更鸟喊道，“也许是命运吧。再说了，我需要我的外套。”<BR><BR>
那天深夜，有人听到他在很远的路那头唱道：<BR><BR>
“哦，特罗布里奇的少女们美丽绝伦......<BR><BR>
......胸如蜜瓜，发似金丝......”<BR>"""

"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
编织之城传说 II：伟大野兽<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
从前，有一只伟大的老虎，霍瓦利的人民崇拜它。戈里乌斯皇帝听说了这件事，勃然大怒，因为崇拜老虎是被禁止的。要知道，在万物初生之时，是阿莱舒特将老虎从它们隐藏的王座上赶下来的。<BR>
<BR>
皇帝将他最心爱、最忠诚的战斗法师，圣师蒂罗·科罗召到身边，对他说：“查出这野兽的真相，用你的狡猾和秘术将它毁灭。”<BR>
<BR>
蒂罗·科罗将自己伪装成一个霍瓦利人，戴着铜珠和桑蚕丝。他乘着一艘哈科小艇，顺尼本大河而下，尼本大河是你的血液，也是尼本纳姆和阿莱舒特的血液。当它因雨水而涨满时，我们的田野是白色的；当它退去时，红米丰收。它的浅滩盛产鱼和螃蟹，它的背脊承载着商人的船队。但要警惕它的情绪和洋流，并防范那些巨大吞噬者的河蛇。<BR>
<BR>
于是，蒂罗·科罗到达了霍瓦利人的祖先之地，位于古老而邪恶的巴纳德尔丛林以西，那里是寇斯林吉人开采银矿的地方。这位受人尊敬的圣师把小艇换成了一头老库塔尔，骑着它前往据说野兽巢穴所在的神殿，那里被称为蒸气针神殿。<BR>
<BR>
他在那里观察到的东西是淫秽且被法律禁止的：每天，霍瓦利人都会来喂养那只伟大而邪恶的老虎，将活人和死人扔进它张开的巨口中。他们还用美酒、用天鹅绒莫克雷调味的红米和石榴来款待它。而野兽津津有味地吞食了一切。霍瓦利人随后会向老虎鞠躬，并宣称它是伟大的神灵，甚至比皇帝本人还要伟大。<BR>
<BR>
但蒂罗·科里，这位狡猾而睿智的圣师技艺大师，设计了一个巧妙的计划。他在河岸上动手，将沥青、毛发和脂肪烘烤成一个人，一个人的形状，他用他的战斗法师秘术使其活过来，直到它与一个血肉之躯的凡人无异。<BR>
<BR>
然后，科罗带着他的造物来到蒸气针神殿，走近老虎，说：“这是给永远饥饿的灵体的美味佳肴。”老虎被自己的食欲蒙蔽了双眼，将那假人整个吞了下去。然后，沥青和脂肪凝结起来，堵塞了野兽的内腔，直到它的肚子裂开，露出了它的粪便。科罗对聚集在那里的霍瓦利人说：“看哪，这就是你们所崇敬的污秽！”人们为他的智慧感到惊奇。<BR>
<BR>
不要崇拜丛林的野兽，那是由谎言和腐烂构成的东西。光界的领域是辉煌灿烂的，没有凡俗的束缚。<BR>"""

"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="500F0F" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
The Talhjolde Companion<BR><FONT COLOR="000000">
published by the<BR>
Imperial University Press, 3E 421<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR>
The Talhjolde, or Song-Stories, represent the strongest link between contemporary Tamrielic society and the Atmoran Nords of so many eras past. This collection has been curated by the Imperial University's Committee for the Transposition of Indigenous Oral Traditions, and serves to keep alive in the minds of both academics and the general public the roots of our culture and shared history.<BR>
<BR>
In this companion to the Talhjolde, different scholars will offer their learned understanding of each tale's origins, meaning and significance. It is important to remember, of course, that these are neither the original Nordic tales nor a serviceable representation of Atmoran totemic religion; they do, however, serve to illustrate the ways in which our mannish origins retain their significance in Tamrielic culture to this day.<BR><BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">I. Hvals Bol (Whale's Sorrow)<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000">- Hakan at-Hatan, Folkloric Linguistics<BR><BR>
There are some odd anachronisms in the language used in this piece. For example, the "fighting twins of old" indubitably refer to the Shield-Thanes of Shor, Tsun and the lesser-known Stuhn (regarded as having left the Nordic pantheon to become Stendarr). However, the Whale in question is the totem of Stuhn, and so there is a strange paradox in likening Whale's emotions to his future representation. This is of course entirely typical of Nordic storytelling, but should highlight to the reader the limitations of applying these modern translations to Mythic Era Atmora.<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">II. Allfathirs Beit (Allfather's Riddle)<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000">- Elvyra Aumilie, Indigenous Oral Traditions<BR><BR>
Riddle-contests and feats of cleverness are very popular in the Nordic oral tradition, and this is exemplary of the genre. Although the character of the "Allfather" or "All-Maker" has either departed mainland Nordic storytelling or been folded into the character of Shor, here we see them as distinct and conflicting characters. In particular, the Fox (Shor's totem) is rebuked for his cleverness at the end, when this kind of wily glory-seeking is most commonly depicted as unambiguous heroism.<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">III. Modiskva Bern (The Angry Bear)<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000">- Batul gra-Brok, Metaphysical History<BR><BR>
The presence of an Adversary in this story has interesting metaphysical implications. I am unaware of many Nordic traditions that have retained this character, barring the most malicious interpretations of Alduin, and it is a concept that challenges traditionally-understood Nordic metaphysics. In particular, it proposes a firm end for Nirn, one that contradicts the kalpic cycle and the existence of a Sovngarde-like reality outside of Mundus.<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">IV. Horsk Olf (Wise Wolf)<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000">- Johannes Silvanus, Indigenous Oral Traditions<BR><BR>
This really is an excellent example of Atmoran and early Nordic songwriting, and it is very exciting to be able to include it in this collection. A few adjustments have been made to ensure rhymes and a consistent meter, but otherwise the spirit of the original song has been captured. The Frost Maiden is one of many archetypes from Atmoran poetry, like Lord Winter or Lady Harvest, whose role has been supplanted by individual heroes of later Nordic storytelling -- not a great loss to some, but I personally miss the timeless quality of these characters.<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">V. Aliga Beit (The Same Question)<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000">- Basil al-Taneth, Tamrielic Migration Studies<BR><BR>
The title here is a play on words that translates well -- it is the "same question" in that it is a question of "sameness", rather than a repetition of some unspoken but pre-existing enquiry. The moral of the tale -- that familiarity is forged and not inherently imbued -- has particular significance for the late Atmoran period, when shifts in climate were forcing disparate Nordic peoples into uneasy coexistence. One should not, however, mistake the answer to this "same question" to be one that Nordic thought has applied freely to the races of Tamriel, as the bloody history of conquest and subjugation post-Atmora demonstrates.<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">VI. Ovaldung Orm (The Snake of Chaos)<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000">- Dagny of the Tower, Skaldic Studies<BR><BR>
Even southerners will generally be familiar with the outline of this story, as it has entered popular mythology and spread through Legion postings and court appointments. It's not known when Orcs were introduced as the victims of Fox's clever thinking, and there is surprisingly little record of conflict between Orcs and early Tamrielic Nords until the Battle of Dragon Wall in 1E660, but it seems likely to have been introduced by skalds from south-eastern Skyrim who had chafed against the predations of Velothi Mountain Orcs in the First Era.<BR>"""
"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="500F0F" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
塔尔霍尔德指南<BR><FONT COLOR="000000">
由<BR>
帝国大学出版社出版，第三纪元421年<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR>
《塔尔霍尔德》，或称《歌谣故事》，代表了当代泰姆瑞尔社会与过去诸多时代的阿特莫拉诺德人之间最紧密的联系。这个集子由帝国大学本土口述传统转写委员会策划，旨在让学术界和公众记住我们文化和共同历史的根源。<BR>
<BR>
在这本《塔尔霍尔德》指南中，不同的学者将对每个故事的起源、意义和重要性提出他们博学的理解。当然，重要的是要记住，这些既不是原始的诺德故事，也不是对阿特莫拉图腾宗教的有用呈现；然而，它们确实有助于说明我们人类起源至今在泰姆瑞尔文化中保持其重要性的方式。<BR><BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">一、赫瓦尔斯·博尔（鲸之悲）<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000"> -- 哈坎·阿特-哈坦，民俗语言学<BR><BR>
这篇作品中使用的语言有一些奇怪的时代错误。例如，“古老的战斗双子”无疑指的是朔尔的持盾家臣，宋恩和鲜为人知的斯图恩（被认为离开了诺德万神殿成为斯滕达尔）。然而，这里所说的鲸是斯图恩的图腾，因此将鲸的情感与其未来的代表相提并论是一个奇怪的悖论。这当然是典型的诺德故事讲述方式，但应向读者强调将这些现代翻译应用于神话纪元的阿特莫拉的局限性。<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">二、阿尔法蒂尔·贝特（众父之谜）<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000"> -- 埃尔维拉·奥米莉，本土口述传统<BR><BR>
谜语竞赛和聪明才智的壮举在诺德口述传统中非常流行，而这是该类型的典范。尽管“众父”或“造物主”的角色要么已从大陆诺德故事讲述中消失，要么被融入了朔尔的角色，但在这里，我们看到他们是不同且冲突的角色。特别是，狐狸（朔尔的图腾）最后因其聪明而受到斥责，而这种狡猾的追求荣耀的行为通常被描绘成毫不含糊的英雄主义。<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">三、莫迪斯克瓦·伯恩（愤怒的熊）<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000"> -- 巴图尔·格拉-布罗克，形而上学历史<BR><BR>
这个故事中对手的存在具有有趣的形而上学含义。除了对奥杜因最恶意的解释外，我不知道有多少诺德传统保留了这一角色，这是一个挑战传统理解的诺德形而上学的概念。特别是，它提出了奈恩的一个确定的终结，一个与劫循环以及梦达斯之外存在类似松加德现实的观念相矛盾的观点。<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">四、霍斯克·奥尔夫（智慧之狼）<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000"> -- 约翰内斯·西尔瓦努斯，本土口述传统<BR><BR>
这确实是阿特莫拉和早期诺德歌曲创作的绝佳范例，能够将其收录进这个集子非常令人兴奋。为了确保押韵和一致的格律，我们做了一些调整，但除此之外，原歌的精神已被捕捉。冰霜少女是阿特莫拉诗歌中的众多原型之一，如冬之主或收获女士，她们的角色已被后来诺德故事讲述中的个别英雄所取代 -- 对某些人来说，这不是什么大损失，但我个人会怀念这些角色的永恒品质。<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">五、阿利加·贝特（同一个问题）<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000"> -- 巴兹尔·阿尔-塔内斯，泰姆瑞尔迁徙研究<BR><BR>
这里的标题是一个翻译得很好的双关语 -- 它是“同一个问题”，因为它是一个关于“同一性”的问题，而不是对某个未说出口但已存在的询问的重复。这个故事的寓意 -- 熟悉感是后天形成的，并非与生俱来 -- 对阿特莫拉晚期尤其重要，当时气候的变化正迫使不同的诺德民族进入不安的共存状态。然而，人们不应误以为这个“同一个问题”的答案是诺德思想自由应用于泰姆瑞尔各民族的，因为阿特莫拉之后征服与征服的流血历史证明了这一点。<BR>
<BR>
<FONT COLOR="500F0F">六、奥瓦顿·奥姆（混沌之蛇）<BR>
<FONT COLOR="000000"> -- 塔楼的达格尼，吟唱诗研究<BR><BR>
即使是南方人通常也会熟悉这个故事的大纲，因为它已进入流行神话，并通过军团驻地和宫廷任命传播开来。不知道兽人是什么时候被引入作为狐狸聪明思维的受害者的，而且令人惊讶的是，直到第一纪元660年的龙墙之战，兽人与早期泰姆瑞尔诺德人之间的冲突记录很少，但这似乎很可能是由来自天际东南部的吟唱诗人引入的，他们在第一纪元曾因维洛提山兽人的掠夺而感到恼怒。<BR>"""

The Talking Guar of Vhul II
弗胡尔会说话的瓜尔 II

"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
The Talking Guar of Vhul: An Analysis<BR>
Book Two: The Investigation<BR>
by Urven Andrelo<BR>
<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
Let us now consider the theories that have been proposed to explain the case of Mudfoot, the talking guar of Vhul.<BR>
<BR>
The most plain explanation is that Balyn, a poor farmer, simply lied and somehow planned the entire occurrence in order to deceive the townsfolk and make some easy coin.<BR>
<BR>
This trickery would have no doubt required some magical ability. And yet, this simple farmer was said to be barely able to speak himself -- let alone make a guar speak. He was almost certainly illiterate, without any education, familial connections, or political ties. Stated plainly, this dull farmer had no means at his disposal to play such a trick.<BR>
<BR>
Surely then, reader, you've considered that some other party was playing a trick on Balyn. Perhaps some unseen wizard crouched in the bushes and staged the initial nix-hound attack, then used magical powers to force a burst of air through the guar's gullet and manipulated its airways just so, playing it like a giant fleshy flute, to create the illusion of speech -- then followed Balyn into town, still unseen, on numerous occasions, to continue the ruse for years?<BR>
<BR>
Let us also consider the amount of arcane talent that would be needed to manipulate the creature as supposed above without immediately killing it. This would require the attention of a very talented (and apparently very bored) wizard. I ask, dear reader, that you consider the following -- what master wizard would bother with such a thing? How astonishingly drunk would a Telvanni mage have to become before dreaming up such a task?<BR>
<BR>
So then let us discuss another possibility, more implausible still, but worth ruling out: perhaps this talking guar was the result of some manner of Daedric trickery? Perhaps the beast was influenced by forces from afar? I see no reason to believe this, simply because the farmer lived for nearly another twenty years after the guar's eventual death, with no apparent madness or tragedy occurring.<BR>
<BR>
The trickster Daedra, such as Sheogorath and his servants, rarely act with much subtlety -- once their game is through, their playthings usually walk no more amongst the living, or are otherwise broken in dramatic fashion. I find it hard to believe that any Daedra would have simply chosen to warn a farmer of a nix-hound attack, then slightly enrich him with petty sums of gold for the next several years, without consequence.<BR>
<BR>
The fourth explanation appears on the surface to be the most reasonable - that the entire story is a fabrication. A legend, a tall tale, a misrembrance told across generations. And indeed, I would assume this to be the case.<BR>
<BR>
 In my quest for answers, however, I have managed to find original correspondence from contemporary witnesses. This does not prove that the story is true -- but it does prove that it is not a modern fabrication, and people of the time did in fact report a talking guar.<BR>
<BR>
In researching this tale, I visited the tax and census office of Old Ebonheart, where Vhul's taxes were processed in Balyn's time. Tax and census data is typically considered to be highly private and restricted, but the records of deceased individuals can be accessed using a Historical Inquiry Request. Say what you will of the Empire's cultural influence in our lands, but they have always proven to be superb record keepers.<BR>
<BR>
I uncovered an official letter from Goras Indavel, a local tax collector whose jurisdiction included Vhul at the time. He wrote a report back to his regional post which mentioned an encounter with "a guar that spoke as a man."<BR>
<BR>
These reports were official documents, and tax collectors were required to report on any irregularities or notable events in the course of performing their duties. Each report was signed under an honor-oath which extended to the financial data logged within. It was thus a high crime against the Tribunal to lie on such a report.<BR>
<BR>
We can then say with a high degree of confidence that Goras Indavel did indeed witness a talking guar -- or at least genuinely believed that he had. There would be no incentive to make such an outlandish claim on an official document. Dated 14th of Rain's Hand, 3E 358, the relevant text states:<BR>
<BR>
"Returned to the inn in Vhul after spending the day collecting dues to the north of the town. Was surprised to meet one Balyn Omathan in the street outside the inn, accepting coins for the display of a guar that spoke as a man. I tossed him a coin out of curiosity, and indeed the creature spoke. It asked me where I was from and even told a dirty joke which I shall not repeat in this dispatch. I must admit I was impressed. I asked Balyn what his trade was -- I had suspected from the roughness of his face that he was a farmer, and I was correct. I shall be visiting farms in his area outside the town tomorrow morning. We shall see if he declares income from his guar."<BR>
<BR>
A seasonal tax record from the following year lists Balyn's trade as "farmer", but also includes a note of "secondary income -- street performer / other". Indeed, only about 60% of Balyn's income seems to have come from farming in that year. It is then safe to conclude that there is some degree of truth to this story.<BR>
<BR>
There was indeed a Dunmer named Balyn Omathan with a guar that seemed to be able to speak, and he profited modestly from this talent for several years. This is the first evidence that I have seen which proves there is any shred of truth to the story at all, and yet it comes so tantalizingly close to an explanation without clarifying anything. <BR>
<BR>
How did this creature speak?<BR>
<BR>
How did it learn to say the things that it is alleged to have said?<BR>
<BR>
Did it think for itself, or was it trained to simply replicate the sounds of speech?<BR>
<BR>
These are questions which shall likely forever perplex me. We now know that Mudfoot the guar did indeed speak -- but the question of how and why he spoke shall most probably always a mystery remain.<BR>"""
"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
弗胡尔会说话的瓜尔：分析<BR>
第二卷：调查<BR>
乌尔文·安德雷洛 著<BR>
<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
现在让我们考虑一下为解释弗胡尔会说话的瓜尔“泥脚”一案而提出的各种理论。<BR>
<BR>
最简单的解释是，巴林，一个贫穷的农民，纯粹是撒谎，并以某种方式策划了整个事件，以欺骗镇民并轻松赚钱。<BR>
<BR>
这种骗局无疑需要一些魔法能力。然而，据说这个简单的农民自己都几乎不会说话 -- 更不用说让瓜尔说话了。他几乎可以肯定是个文盲，没有任何教育、家庭关系或政治联系。简而言之，这个迟钝的农民没有办法施展这样的诡计。<BR>
<BR>
那么，读者，你一定想过，是其他某个角色在戏弄巴林。也许某个看不见的巫师蹲在灌木丛中，策划了最初的尼克斯犬袭击，然后使用魔法迫使一股空气通过瓜尔的喉咙，并如此操纵它的气道，像吹奏巨大的肉笛一样，创造出说话的幻觉 -- 然后，仍然不被看见，多次跟随巴林进城，将这种欺骗持续多年？<BR>
<BR>
让我们也考虑一下，要像上面假设的那样操纵那只生物而不立即杀死它，需要多少神秘天赋。这将需要一位非常有天赋（而且显然非常无聊）的巫师的关注。我请亲爱的读者考虑以下问题 -- 哪个大师级的巫师会费心做这种事？一个泰瓦尼法师要醉到什么程度才会想出这样的任务？<BR>
<BR>
那么，让我们讨论另一种可能性，更加难以置信，但值得排除：也许这只会说话的瓜尔是某种迪德拉诡计的结果？也许这头野兽受到了来自远方的力量的影响？我看不出有什么理由相信这一点，仅仅是因为那个农民在瓜尔最终死后又活了将近二十年，没有发生明显的疯狂或悲剧。<BR>
<BR>
像谢尔格拉斯和他的仆从这样的恶作剧迪德拉，很少会非常巧妙地行动 -- 一旦他们的游戏结束，他们的玩物通常不会再在生者中行走，或者会以戏剧性的方式被摧毁。我很难相信任何迪德拉会简单地选择警告一个农民尼克斯犬的袭击，然后在接下来的几年里用少量黄金稍微让他富有，而不产生任何后果。<BR>
<BR>
第四个解释表面上看起来最合理 -- 整个故事是捏造的。一个传说，一个夸张的故事，一个代代相传的误记。事实上，我会假设情况就是这样。<BR>
<BR>
然而，在我寻求答案的过程中，我设法找到了当时目击者的原始信件。这并不能证明这个故事是真的 -- 但它确实证明这不是现代捏造的，当时的人们确实报告过一只会说话的瓜尔。<BR>
<BR>
在研究这个故事时，我访问了旧黑檀心的税收和人口普查办公室，巴林时代弗胡尔的税收就是在那里处理的。税收和人口普查数据通常被认为是高度私密和受限的，但可以通过历史调查请求访问已故个人的记录。你可以随意评价帝国在我们土地上的文化影响，但事实一再证明，他们是杰出的记录保存者。<BR>
<BR>
我发现了一封来自当时管辖范围包括弗胡尔的本地收税员戈拉斯·因达维尔的官方信件。他写了一份报告给他的地区职位，其中提到遇到“一只能像人一样说话的瓜尔”。<BR>
<BR>
这些报告是官方文件，收税员被要求在履行职责过程中报告任何违规或值得注意的事件。每份报告都是在荣誉誓言下签署的，该誓言也适用于其中记录的财务数据。因此，在这种报告上撒谎是对审判席的严重犯罪。<BR>
<BR>
那么，我们可以高度确信地说，戈拉斯·因达维尔确实目睹了一只会说话的瓜尔 -- 或者至少真诚地相信他看到了。在官方文件上做出如此古怪的声称是没有动机的。日期为第三纪元358年，雨手月14日，相关文本指出：<BR>
<BR>
“在镇北收取税款一天后，回到了弗胡尔的客栈。惊讶地在客栈外的街上遇到一个名叫巴林·奥马森的人，他正接受硬币以展示一只能像人一样说话的瓜尔。出于好奇，我扔给他一枚硬币，那生物确实说话了。它问我从哪里来，甚至还讲了一个黄色笑话，我不会在这份急件中重复。我必须承认我印象深刻。我问巴林他是做什么的 -- 从他粗糙的面相我怀疑他是个农民，我猜对了。明天早上我将去他镇外的农场区域视察。我们将看看他是否会申报来自他瓜尔的收入。”<BR>
<BR>
第二年的季度税收记录将巴林的职业列为“农民”，但也包括一条注释：“次要收入 -- 街头表演者/其他”。事实上，在那一年，巴林只有大约60%的收入似乎来自农业。那么可以安全地得出结论，这个故事有一定程度的真实性。<BR>
<BR>
确实有一个名叫巴林·奥马森的丹莫，他有一只似乎会说话的瓜尔，并且他靠这个才能赚了些钱好几年。这是我见过的第一个证据，证明这个故事确实有一丝真实性，然而它却如此诱人地接近解释，却没有澄清任何事情。<BR>
<BR>
这个生物是如何说话的？<BR>
<BR>
它是如何学会说那些据称它说过的话的？<BR>
<BR>
它是自己思考，还是仅仅被训练来复制声音？<BR>
<BR>
这些问题可能永远会让我困惑。我们现在知道瓜尔“泥脚”确实会说话 -- 但它如何以及为何会说话的问题，很可能将永远是一个谜。<BR>"""

The Talking Guar of Vhul I
弗胡尔会说话的瓜尔 I

> BOOK.TEXT T_Bk_TalkingGuarOfVhul_ITR
"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
The Talking Guar of Vhul: An Analysis<BR>
Book One: The Tale<BR>
by Urven Andrelo<BR>
<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
There are a great many beasts in Mundus known to speak, but the simple guar is certainly not counted among them. One glance into its oafish eyes reveals this to be indisputably true. And yet, there is a tale to be told of Mudfoot, the talking guar of Vhul.<BR>
<BR>
There are many accounts from supposed witnesses, but with the passage of time it has become nearly impossible to strain the dewdrops of truth from the coagulated sap of rumor and jest. Indeed, this story is of personal importance to me -- having heard the story countless times as a youth, yet never seeing any evidence as to its veracity, I've long yearned to get to the bottom of this local historical curiosity. My own grandfather is said to have witnessed the speaking guar himself in his time, but as he was killed in the Arnesian War when I was young, I never had the chance to hear him tell of it.<BR>
<BR>
Our tale begins with Balyn Omathan, a poor whickweat farmer living in a simple shack in the mucklands southwest of Vhul. Thus goes the story -- one morning, as Balyn began setting about his work of crawling through the mud to prune his whickweat stalks, he heard a huffing and puffing (or perhaps a scuffling and chuffling) behind his back.<BR>
<BR>
He turned in time to see his guar Mudfoot a few dozen paces away, frantically hopping up and down, calling out "Beware! Beware!". As alarming as this sight surely must have been, Balyn was a bit more immediately concerned with the massive nix-hound that had latched onto his shoulder. It tore into his flesh with its mandibles, but Balyn was able to return the insult by sliding his rusty whickweat knife into the beast's proboscis. He was wounded, but not terribly so, and his dull hooked blade had been enough to drive the creature away.<BR>
<BR>
Balyn was shaking still as he bandaged himself within the safety of his shack when he remembered that his guar had spoken. He was perplexed, and rightly so, for when he approached the beast and rubbed its great snout, it would not speak again. Had he imagined it? Was he losing his mind?<BR>
<BR>
Several days later, Balyn traveled into the town of Vhul with Mudfoot, who pulled his heavy whickweat cart to market. And a strange thing happened - Mudfoot began to greet the townsfolk as they walked past. "Hello!", "Good day!" he called out as people walked past, stopping them in their tracks.<BR>
<BR>
Soon a crowd had gathered to see the talking guar. Balyn sold every single stalk of his whickweat that day, and was delighted to return to his farm with a light cart and a heavy coinpurse. TELEPORTATION: PREMISE & PRAXIS - Vol. I<BR>

Self-catalyzed, instantaneous teleportation was long believed to be an unattainable dream, a fancy of folktales -- god-heroes riding the winds of Kyne, armies transported to distant lands, or unlucky folk vanishing into Oblivion by the will of evil spirits.

DOORS OF OBLIVION<BR>
<BR>The earliest known method of teleportation was to plot a course through Oblivion. Odd gateways link the planes of Oblivion, and those with knowledge of such connections could use them to quickly travel from one mundane location to another.
<BR>

传送：前提与实践 - 卷一<BR>
沃甘娜·普洛提努斯 著<BR>

<BR>传送的首次成功验证是通过精密的引擎实现的，例如亚蒂莱·迪伦尼的遮蔽隧道。这些隧道需要数周的神秘计算以及大量的以太物质 -- 事实上，数量如此之多，以至于著名的莱恩·迪伦尼本人将其嘲笑为想象中最慢、最昂贵的旅行方法。

One practitioner of such magics, the eastern mage Barilzar, was supposedly capable of easily rending the divisions between planes of existence, bypassing the various limits of other methods entirely.
<BR>
Barilzar did not need to visit his destination beforehand, required no calculations other than his will and desires, and used no instruments other than arcane artifacts whose functionality could be used even by a novice. In this way, he could summon creatures and objects from even the most secure planes and travel wherever he wished.
<BR>
Barilzar disappeared during the Second Interregnum, taking the secret of his technique with him. Other explorations into the teleportation potential of the Dawn Magics have ended in disaster, prompting Imperial authorities to prohibit further study of the subject.
<BR>
As is typical where the study of the Dawn Magics is concerned, some scholars have claimed a connection to the elven cultures of the Merethic Era, speculating that these early peoples had access to the Dawn Arts, using them in the colonization and exploration of primordial Tamriel. The supposed wars of Altmora, and the seemingly erratic movements of the Falmer and Dwemer populations are often brought up, as are the strange mentions of Kyne-winds in early Nordic myth. It goes without saying that there is not a shred of archeological evidence to support such claims.
<BR>
INTERVENTION<BR>
<BR>More familiar to the reader, no doubt, are intervention spells, which are first mentioned in the First Interregnum. Cyrodiilic hagiographies of this period attribute the rescue of various imperiled saints to acts of the gods, who, by way of their awesome power, take these hapless pilgrims away from danger or imprisonment and deposit them safely in some holy place, which inevitably became a temple or place of pilgrimage.
<BR>
Strangely, intervention spells appear to have been completely unknown to the Alessians, but became relatively commonplace by the reign of Reman. They were overwhelmingly (though not exclusively) associated with temples of the Eight Divines, which saw a large resurgence during the Interregnum.
<BR>
The Divine nature of these spells is uncertain. They function much like other spells, drawing on a person's natural wellsprings of magicka. It may be that Intervention is merely a hierophant's clever obfuscation of a spell in meaningless ritual brocade, much like modern mages such as Ondusi, who add vestigial flourishes in order to trademark and protect their licenses.
<BR>
Indeed, scrolls and spells of Divine Intervention work just as well in the hands of a secular-minded caster as in those of a priest. Variants of Intervention also exist, such as the Baandari Self-Theft scrolls, spells addressing the heathen Tribunes of Morrowind, and even scroll variants for the Altmer and Direnni market invoking elven deities.
<BR>
That being said, the precise effects of Intervention still have not been replicated in an entirely secular context. It is possible these spells draw on an essential part of the mortal psyche, the faith in their Gods, or their desire for the safety of a holy place.<BR>"""
"""<DIV ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT COLOR="000000" SIZE="3" FACE="Magic Cards"><BR>
传送：前提与实践 - 卷二<BR>
沃甘娜·普洛提努斯 著<BR>
<DIV ALIGN="LEFT"><BR><BR>
在前一卷中，我们考虑了我们祖先使用湮灭的旁路和各种神秘机器对传送魔法的早期尝试。在描述当代实践之前，我们必须首先研究另外两种方法，它们在全盛时期是在第一纪元晚期和共同纪元。
<BR>
黎明魔法<BR>
<BR>除了通过虚空通道和使用奇怪的引擎，前塞劳丁时代最常被引用的第三种传送方法是使用黎明魔法，那些可以追溯到世界最原始状态的晦涩艺术。
<BR>
这种魔法的一位实践者，东方法师巴里尔扎，据称能够轻易撕裂存在位面之间的分隔，完全绕开其他方法的种种限制。
<BR>
巴里尔扎不需要事先访问他的目的地，除了他的意志和欲望外不需要任何计算，并且除了即使新手也能使用的神秘神器外不使用任何工具。通过这种方式，他可以从甚至最安全的位面召唤生物和物体，并随心所欲地旅行到任何地方。
<BR>
巴里尔扎在第二次大空位期消失了，带走了他的技术秘密。其他关于黎明魔法传送潜力的探索都以灾难告终，促使帝国当局禁止进一步研究该主题。
<BR>
就像研究黎明魔法时常见的那样，一些学者声称这与精灵纪元时代的精灵文化有关，推测这些早期民族能够使用黎明技艺，并将其用于原始泰姆瑞尔的殖民和探索。所谓的阿尔特莫拉战争，以及伐莫和锻莫人群看似不规律的活动，常常被提起，早期诺德神话中对吉讷之风的奇怪提及也是如此。不用说，没有一丝考古证据支持这些说法。
<BR>
神佑干涉<BR>
<BR>毫无疑问，读者更熟悉的是神佑干涉法术，它们首次出现在第一次大空位期。这一时期西罗帝尔的圣徒传记将各种遇险圣徒的获救归功于众神的行动，众神以其强大的力量将这些不幸的朝圣者从危险或囚禁中带走，并将他们安全地安置在某处圣地，这不可避免地成为了一座神殿或朝圣地。
<BR>
奇怪的是，神佑干涉法术似乎对阿莱西亚人完全未知，但在雷曼统治时期变得相对普遍。它们绝大多数（尽管并非全部）与八圣灵的神殿有关，这些神殿在大空位期经历了大规模的复兴。
<BR>
这些法术的神圣性是不确定的。它们的功能很像其他法术，利用一个人天生的魔能源泉。也许神佑干涉仅仅是圣师将法术巧妙地隐藏在无意义的仪式锦缎中，就像现代法师如昂杜西，为了商标和保护他们的许可证而添加退化的修饰。
<BR>
事实上，神佑干涉的卷轴和法术在世俗思想的施法者手中和在祭司手中一样有效。神佑干涉也存在变体，例如班达隶自盗卷轴，针对晨风异教审判席的法术，甚至还有为傲特莫和迪伦尼市场制作的、祈求精灵神祇的卷轴变体。
<BR>
话虽如此，神佑干涉的确切效果仍然未能在完全世俗的背景下复制。这些法术可能利用了凡人心理的一个基本部分，即对他们神祇的信仰，或对圣地安全的渴望。<BR>"""

THE CELAUDINE METHOD<BR>

At the time, the question of self-catalyzed teleportation had - literally - consumed Breton academia for decades, with many of Gwylim's best and brightest falling victim to ill-conceived arcane mishaps. Gwylim's Twist Hall, with its petrified figures and fused horrors, remains a sobering reminder of the risks our predecessors took in developing spells we now take for granted.

It took another two decades after Celaud's death for his assistant to transcribe and refine the spells into a functional and practical shape.

As such, early practitioners of teleportation were often persecuted, and until the re-establishment of trans-provincial scholarship under the Septimite Mages Guild renewals, it remained an obscure and suspicious practice.<BR>"""
